doc.title: Henry Johnson interviewed by Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 30, 1995

title: Blues, shared experience and the value of music education
summary: Experience behind the blues, music as outlet for pain, audiences identifying with Joe's songs, cuts to school arts and the Oklahoma City bombing remark.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: Yeah, I agree with you. I agree with you yeah. It does make a great difference.

You know you talk about for instance you talk about knowing the lyrics. But also it’s like if the music is expensive to you, if that costs you something, experientially, to embody that. You know you talk about the blues. You know, well you know if a guy pulls up in his Ferrari Testarossa, you know, at his girl friend’s house, it’s going to be hard for him to sing the blues and convince me. You know what I’m saying? I don’t know if he ever had the blues. He might know the twelve bar progression. You know what I’m saying? Now give us an example of that, or how that, working with Joe has given you any of those examples.

Well, that’s sort of intrinsic to point out. But most all the blues were written about, or written from somebody’s experience. And since we are all human beings, no matter what color you are or where you’re from, you’re going to experience some pain and sorrow in your life because that is a part of living. You know those things happen to us to learn how to deal with our emotions. And musicians have a great outlet for that. You know we can deal with ours just by singing about it and telling you about it, and then it doesn’t make us feel so bad. But the poor people that are not musicians and they’re just day to day, they don’t have an outlet for that. So that’s where we come in. So they can listen to us and identify with something that just happened to them, and they’ll say, well I guess I’m not the only one. It doesn’t make them feel lonely anymore, like they’re the only one that this would happen to. I mean there’s a lot of times when we’re out there and we’re playing

shows, and Joe will sing a song and people, I just see people melt. Because they identify with it right away. And it just makes you feel like you’re a part of the whole and not an outsider and out there by yourself. You know and I think that has a great effect on everything in society. So we were talking about something the other day about this school program. I remember when I came up in school, music was an integral part and the arts were an integral part of everything. And by them trying to cut that out now I think is one of the greatest sins they could do.

Let me ask you this question. Because I asked somebody else this. And I’m going to make a statement and then you just kind of jump in on it. That is, you know the guy that set the bomb in Oklahoma City? I don’t think that that guy could have done that if he had even that same morning listened to a Mozart or a Mendelssohn symphony or listened to a couple of good tracks by Ellington.

That’s right. I agree with you there. I mean there’s certain kinds of music that will pull up that violent nature in you. I won’t mention any names, but there are those musics out there. And then there’s other musics that soothe you and make you feel like you’re a part of everybody. And the ones that make you feel like you’re a part of everybody would never make you do those kinds of things.
